latest_release.body:
## Behavior changes: read before upgrading

### Output from an HTTP log handler

Security advisory: [GHSA-r6wq-r8rh-6rc3](https://github.com/matsumotory/ngx_mruby/security/advisories/GHSA-r6wq-r8rh-6rc3).

- Before: a log handler could append the text of `Nginx.rputs` or `Nginx.echo` after the response body.
- Now: the calls convert their argument as usual and write no bytes. The script continues after a successful call.
- Why it changed:
  - The defect: the shared handler finalizer could flush an output chain while nginx was freeing the request.
  - Why the old behavior could not be kept: extra bytes could be read as another response on the connection.
  - What the documentation promised: the [log directives](../directives/README.md#mruby_log_handler-and-mruby_log_handler_code) run at the end of request processing for logging.
- Affected: HTTP file and inline log handlers, including calls from their helper methods.
- What to do: log messages with `Nginx.log`. Write response bodies in a content handler.
- Not changed by this release: argument conversion errors and output from ordinary content handlers.

### Output of an mruby content handler or body filter in an SSI subrequest

Security advisory: [GHSA-79vp-37cx-547v](https://github.com/matsumotory/ngx_mruby/security/advisories/GHSA-79vp-37cx-547v).

- Before: the output of a subrequest's mruby content handler (`Nginx.rputs`, `Nginx.echo`, `Nginx.send_header`) or mruby body filter could end the parent response at the subrequest's output. Over HTTP/1.1 the chunked filter emitted the response-terminator chunk mid-stream, so a length-delimited reader saw two responses where there was one; over HTTP/1.0 or when the parent used `Content-Length`, the parent response was cut short at the subrequest's bytes and the connection closed; and a static file read through the mruby body filter of a subrequest held the main request until `send_timeout`.
- Now: a subrequest marks its last buffer with `last_in_chain` (and `sync` for an empty buffer), as nginx's own handlers do. The parent response goes on until the main request's own last buffer. The static file case no longer stops the main request.
- Why it changed:
  - The defect: ngx_mruby's response finalization set `last_buf` on every chain, which is correct only for the main request. Nginx's chunked filter, Content-Length framing and body-end detection act on `last_buf`.
  - Why the old behavior could not be kept: a subrequest's `last_buf` ended the parent response early (a split chunked response, a truncated Content-Length or HTTP/1.0 response, read as another response on a shared connection), and the body-filter path held the main request until `send_timeout` closed the connection.
  - What the documentation promised: [Nginx.rputs](https://github.com/matsumotory/ngx_mruby/blob/v2.7.5/docs/class_and_method/README.md#nginxrputsstring) and [Nginx::Filter](https://github.com/matsumotory/ngx_mruby/blob/v2.7.5/docs/class_and_method/README.md#nginxfilter-class) in 2.7.5 said nothing about how a subrequest's output interacts with the parent response.
- Affected: locations whose mruby content handler calls `Nginx.rputs`, `Nginx.echo` or `Nginx.send_header`, or whose mruby body filter produces a body, when another location includes them with SSI `<!--# include virtual=... -->` or by another form of subrequest.
- What to do: nothing. The subrequest output is framed correctly as part of the parent response.

### A value of mruby_set or Nginx::Var whose to_s is missing, raises or does not return a String no longer ends the worker (#768)

- Before: ngx_mruby converted a value that is not a String with its `to_s` and used the result as a String without checking its type. For the value that the code of `mruby_set` or `mruby_set_code` returned, it called `to_s` where mruby does not raise an exception of `to_s` but returns it. detail.readme:
ngx_mruby: A Fast and Memory-Efficient Nginx Extension Mechanism Scripting with mruby.

## Documents - [Install](https://github.com/matsumotory/ngx_mruby/tree/master/docs/install) - [Test](https://github.com/matsumotory/ngx_mruby/tree/master/docs/test) - [Directives](https://github.com/matsumotory/ngx_mruby/tree/master/docs/directives) - [Class and Method](https://github.com/matsumotory/ngx_mruby/tree/master/docs/class_and_method) - [Use Case](https://github.com/matsumotory/ngx_mruby/tree/master/docs/use_case) - [Release notes (behaviour changes to read before upgrading)](https://github.com/matsumotory/ngx_mruby/tree/master/docs/releases) - [Trust boundary](https://github.com/matsumotory/ngx_mruby/blob/master/docs/README.md#trust-boundary): the configuration and its Ruby code are trusted, what a client sends is not, and what each side is responsible for - [Examples](https://github.com/hsbt/nginx-tech-talk) ## Branch strategy ngx_mruby has three long-lived code branches: `master`, `next` and `v2.x`. Their names and roles stay as they are. `master` is the 2.x line until v3 is promoted to it, so that everyone who builds from the default branch keeps receiving the 2.x security fixes. v3 is developed on `next` and becomes `master` at v3.0.0 (the promotion). From then on, `v2.x` carries 2.x. The site, [ngx.mruby.org](https://ngx.mruby.org/), is built from `docs/` by `.github/workflows/site.yml` on `next` and deployed by GitHub Actions: 3.x from `next` at the unprefixed paths, 2.x from `master` under `/v2/`. The `gh-pages` branch keeps the old site as history. ```text until the promotion | after the promotion | next ---*alpha.1---*beta.1---*rc.1---*rc.N---+ | - - ? \ master -*v2.7.0--*v2.7.x-- ... -----------o------M------*------*--- ... --> 3.x : : : v2.x -*v2.7.0--*v2.7.x-- ... -----------o----------*------*------ ... --] 2.x * a release tag (v2.*, v3.*) or a pre-release tag (v3.0.0-*); v2.7.x stands for the 2.x releases after v2.7.0 o the last 2.x commit on master : the same commit on both branches M the merge of next into master, tagged v3.0.0 ? what next becomes after the promotion is open (see the table below) ] the end of 2.x support, twelve months after v3.0.0 The merges of master into next before the promotion are not drawn. ``` | Branch | Until the promotion | After the promotion (v3.0.0) | |---|---|---| | `master` (default branch) | The 2.x line: 2.x fixes, `v2.*` releases | The 3.x line: `v3.*` releases | | `v2.x` | The same commits as `master`: a workflow copies every push to `master` to `v2.x` | The 2.x line: stability and security fixes, `v2.*` releases | | `next` | Development of v3 and its pre-releases | Open; the recommendation is to keep it for the development of 3.1 (see [Promoting v3 to master](docs/DEVELOPMENT.md#promoting-v3-to-master)) | Until the promotion, `master` is merged into `next` after 2.x fixes, so v3 has them too. v3 is developed on `next`. Its pre-releases are tagged `v3.0.0-alpha.N`, `v3.0.0-beta.N` and `v3.0.0-rc.N` and are marked as pre-releases on GitHub. Section 6 of the v3 plan ([docs/proposals/v3-plan.md](https://github.com/matsumotory/ngx_mruby/blob/next/docs/proposals/v3-plan.md) on `next`) sets when the first pre-release of each kind is tagged: - `v3.0.0-alpha.1`: when the 2.x test suite passes on the new core of v3 and the sanitizers report nothing. - `v3.0.0-beta.1`: when the migration guide and the examples exist. - `v3.0.0-rc.1`: when the site and the examples are complete. `v3.0.0` is tagged when `next` is promoted to `master`, under the conditions in [Promoting v3 to master](docs/DEVELOPMENT.md#promoting-v3-to-master). No date is set. At least one `v3.0.0-rc.N` comes first, and how long the last one stays out before v3.0.0 is still open. The pre-releases and releases appear on the [releases page](https://github.com/matsumotory/ngx_mruby/releases); to be notified of them, watch the repository with "Custom" and "Releases" selected. ### For existing users If you do not want anything to change, build from `v2.x` or from the latest `v2.*` release tag instead of `master`, and switch now: ```sh git clone -b v2.x https://github.com/matsumotory/ngx_mruby.git # the 2.x branch git clone -b vX.Y.Z https://github.com/matsumotory/ngx_mruby.git # or the latest v2.* release tag ``` A release tag does not receive fixes. If you pin one, move to each new 2.x release, because only the latest 2.x release is supported (see [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md#supported-versions)), or pin `v2.x`, which receives the 2.x fixes as they are merged. If you start using ngx_mruby now, the same applies: for production, build from `v2.x` or the latest `v2.*` release tag, and to try v3, track `next`. Until the promotion, `v2.x` has the same commits as `master`, so pinning it does not change the code you build until then. At the promotion, `master` becomes v3.0.0, a new major version. Section 7 of the [v3 plan](https://github.com/matsumotory/ngx_mruby/blob/next/docs/proposals/v3-plan.md) already decides changes to its build requirements and behavior: mruby 4.1 instead of 3.3; nginx 1.30 (stable) and 1.31 (mainline) as the oldest supported versions, raised every April, so that users of older nginx stay on 2.x (2.x builds with nginx 1.28 and 1.26, and with nginx 1.24, which Linux distributions package, only without stream, that is, without `--with-stream`); OpenSSL 3.5 as the baseline with 1.1.1 and 3.0 dropped; `auto-ssl` removed from the default build; and the behavior changes of item 8: a Ruby API called outside the phase it is designed for raises an exception, an exception after `rputs` returns 500, `Headers#delete` matches the full header name, `Nginx.return 200` with an empty body is allowed, and a body is sent with any status. The [v3 migration guide](https://github.com/matsumotory/ngx_mruby/blob/next/docs/migration/README.md) on `next` lists each of these changes once it is merged there. The 2.x line (`master` until the promotion, then `v2.x`) puts compatibility first. It receives only stability fixes (crashes, hangs, leaks, and build fixes such as those for new nginx, OS, compiler or OpenSSL releases) and security fixes, and it changes behavior only as far as the fix of a defect requires. Since 2.7.1, the release notes in [docs/releases/](docs/releases/) list each such change. 2.x stays supported for twelve months after v3.0.0 (see [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md#supported-versions)). Releases are tagged `vX.Y.Z`. If you contribute a fix, send 2.x fixes to `master` until the promotion and v3 work to `next` (see [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#branches-and-pull-requests)). Before upgrading, read the "Behavior changes: read before upgrading" section of every newer release in [docs/releases/](docs/releases/). Please report security vulnerabilities privately as described in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). The project has earned the passing level of the [OpenSSF Best Practices badge](https://www.bestpractices.dev/projects/16057). ## What's ngx_mruby __ngx_mruby is A Fast and Memory-Efficient TCP/UDP Load Balancing and Web Server Extension Mechanism Using Scripting Language mruby for nginx.__ - ngx_mruby is to provide an alternative to lua-nginx-module or [mod_mruby of Apache httpd](http://mod.mruby.org/). - Unified Ruby Code between Apache(mod_mruby), nginx(ngx_mruby) and other Web server software(plan) for Web server extensions. - You can implement nginx modules by Ruby scripts on nginx! - You can implement some Web server software extensions by same Ruby code (as possible) - Supported nginx main-line and stable-line - [Benchmark between ngx_mruby and lua-nginx-module](https://www.techempower.com/benchmarks/#section=data-r10&hw=peak&test=plaintext&w=4-0) ```ruby # location /proxy { # mruby_set $backend "/path/to/proxy.rb"; # proxy_pass http://$backend; # } backends = [ "test1", "test2", "test3", ] r = Redis.new "192.168.12.251", 6379 r.get backends[rand(backends.length)] ``` This example needs the `Redis` class of mruby-redis, and a running Redis server. The default `build_config.rb` builds mruby-redis again since 2.7.2; 2.7.1 left it out. - see [examples](https://github.com/matsumotory/ngx_mruby/blob/master/example/nginx.conf) - __Sample of Unified Ruby Code between Apache(mod_mruby) and nginx(ngx_mruby) for Web server extensions__ - You can implement some Web server software extensions by same Ruby code (as possible) ```ruby # Unified Ruby Code between Apache(mod_mruby) and nginx(ngx_mruby) # for Web server extensions. # # Apache httpd.conf by mod_mruby # # # mrubyHandlerMiddle "/path/to/unified_hello.rb" # # # nginx nginx.conf by ngx_mruby # # location /mruby { # mruby_content_handler "/path/to/unified_hello.rb"; # } # Server = get_server_class Server::rputs "Hello #{Server::module_name}/#{Server::module_version} world!" # mod_mruby => "Hello mod_mruby/0.9.3 world!" # ngx_mruby => "Hello ngx_mruby/0.0.1 world!" ``` [![ngx_mruby mod_mruby performance](https://github.com/matsumotory/mod_mruby/raw/master/images/performance_20140301.png)](http://blog.matsumoto-r.jp/?p=3974) ※ [hello world simple benchmark, see details of blog entry.](http://blog.matsumoto-r.jp/?p=3974) ## Abstract As the increase of large-scale and complex Web services, not only the development of Web applications is required, but also the implementation of Web server extensions in many cases. Most Web server extensions are mainly implemented in the C language because of fast and memory-efficient behavior, but by writing extensions using a scripting language we can achieve better maintainability and productivity. However, if the existing methods are primarily intended to enhance not the implementation of Web applications but the implementation of internal processing of the Web server, the problem remains in terms of speed, memory-efficiency and safety. Therefore, we propose a fast and memory-efficient Web server extension mechanism using a scripting language. We designed an architecture where the server process creates a region in memory to save the state of the interpreter at the server process startup, and multiple scripts share this region to process the scripts quickly when new request are made. The server process frees the global variables table, the exception flag and the byte-code which cause an increase of memory usage, in order to reduce the memory usage and extend safety by preventing interference between each script because of sharing the region. We implemented a mechanism that can extend the internal processing of nginx easily by Ruby scripts using nginx and the embeddable scripting language mruby. It's called "ngx_mruby". ### What a worker keeps between requests The abstract above describes the design of the paper. ngx_mruby today does not free the global variables table between scripts. nginx creates one `mrb_state` for the `http {}` block (and one for the `stream {}` block) while it reads the configuration, and runs the init code (`mruby_init`, `mruby_stream_init`) and the server configuration code (`mruby_server_context_handler_code`) in it before it starts the workers, in the master process. Each worker process gets its own copy when nginx forks it, and runs all the other mruby code of the block in that copy: the init_worker and exit_worker code and every handler and filter, in every server and location, for every client. A reload or a restart starts new workers with a new state. Global variables, constants, instance variables of `main` (the `self` of handler code), methods defined with `def`, classes and modules with their constants, and what `Userdata` holds (it keeps its values in a global variable) stay in the worker from one request to the next. What one request leaves behind is seen by every later request that the same worker handles, also when the code raised an exception after it made the change. Each worker has its own copy, so one worker does not see the values of another. After each run, ngx_mruby clears the exception (`mrb->exc`); a script file without `cache` is read and compiled again for the next run, and inline code and cached scripts keep the byte-code compiled at startup. The garbage collector frees the objects that nothing refers to any more. Local variables do not stay: each run of handler code starts without them. Do not keep the data of one request in global variables, constants, instance variables of `main` or `Userdata`, since the next request of the worker, from any client, sees it. Use local variables, and read and write the request through `Nginx::Request`, `Nginx::Var`, `Nginx::Headers_in` and `Nginx::Headers_out` (in `stream {}`, where code runs per session, `Nginx::Stream::Connection`). To pass data from one handler to a later handler of the same request, declare an nginx variable with `set $name "";` and read and write it through `Nginx::Var`, or set the `Userdata` value in every request before it is read. A `set` in the location runs after `mruby_rewrite_handler` and empties the variable again, so declare a variable that a rewrite handler writes with `set` in the `server {}` block. Keep in globals and constants only what all requests of the worker are meant to share, such as settings that the init or init_worker code prepares. [`Nginx.remove_global_variable`](docs/class_and_method/README.md#nginxremove_global_variable) removes a global variable. # Contributions This project exists thanks to all the people who contribute. We also welcome financial contributions in full transparency on our [open collective](https://opencollective.com/ngx_mruby). ## Backers Thank you to all our backers! 🙏 [[Become a backer](https://opencollective.com/ngx_mruby#backer)] ## Sponsors Support this project by becoming a sponsor.
